items.stem: What is meant by ethics in computing?
options: The speed of a computer
The laws about copyright
Rules of a programming language
Moral principles that guide the behaviour of computing professionals
items.answer: Moral principles that guide the behaviour of computing professionals
items.markingKey: Ethics: what is right/wrong in professional conduct.

items.stem: What does BCS stand for?
options: British Computer Software
British Computer Society (The Chartered Institute for IT)
Basic Computer Standards
Binary Coded Systems
items.answer: British Computer Society (The Chartered Institute for IT)
items.markingKey: BCS has a code of conduct for IT professionals.

items.stem: Explain why a software engineer should only accept work they are competent to do.
items.answer: Lack of competence could lead to faulty software that harms clients or the public; the code requires professional competence and honesty about limitations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: risk of harm/poor work; 1 mark: duty of competence/integrity [2]

items.stem: Grace is asked to collect more personal data from users of an app made by MetroBus than the app needs. Discuss the ethical issues involved.
items.answer: Privacy of users, informed consent, data protection law; the code requires respect for privacy and acting in the public interest; Grace should challenge the request and collect only necessary data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per relevant issue, max 3 [3]

items.stem: Priya is joining Horizon Travel as a junior software engineer. Discuss the importance of professional codes of conduct for programmers working on safety-critical systems.
items.answer: Points in favour: codes require competence, honesty, public interest; reduce risks to life; maintain public trust; guide difficult decisions. Points against / limitations: codes are not legally binding; membership is voluntary; commercial pressure may override them; codes are general and need interpretation. Conclusion: codes are valuable but must be backed by law, testing standards and company culture.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 2 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. Indicative content: codes require competence, honesty, public interest; reduce risks to life; maintain public trust; guide difficult decisions. / codes are not legally binding; membership is voluntary; commercial pressure may override them; codes are general and need interpretation. [4]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which is a principle in the BCS code of conduct? (b) Why do professional bodies publish codes of conduct?
items.answer: (a) Act in the public interest (b) To set standards of professional behaviour that members are expected to follow
items.markingKey: (a) BCS principles: public interest, professional competence and integrity, duty to relevant authority, duty to the profession. (b) Codes guide decisions and protect the public and the reputation of the profession.

items.stem: Explain one way in which acting in the public interest might conflict with an employer's wishes.
items.answer: An employer may want to release software quickly with known safety or security flaws; the engineer's duty to the public requires the risk to be reported or the release delayed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: example conflict; 1 mark: public interest outweighs employer [2]

items.stem: Chloe is asked to sign off testing for software at Palm Grove Hotel that has not been tested. Explain why this would be unethical.
items.answer: It is dishonest and could put users at risk; codes require honesty and professional competence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: dishonesty/risk; 1 mark: principle [2]

items.stem: Jonas is asked to collect more personal data from users of an app made by SkyLink Airways than the app needs. Discuss the ethical issues involved.
items.answer: Privacy of users, informed consent, data protection law; the code requires respect for privacy and acting in the public interest; Jonas should challenge the request and collect only necessary data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per relevant issue, max 3 [3]

items.stem: Daniel is offered a gift by a supplier while choosing software for Horizon Travel. Explain why accepting it could breach a code of conduct.
items.answer: It creates a conflict of interest and may bias the decision; codes require integrity and honest, impartial judgement in the employer's interest.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conflict of interest; 1 mark: integrity/impartiality [2]

items.stem: A manager at Coral Bay Aquarium asks Arjun to copy code from a competitor's product found online. Explain why this is unethical and what Arjun should do.
items.answer: It breaches copyright and professional integrity; Arjun should refuse, explain the legal and ethical issues and suggest writing original code or licensing the code.

items.stem: What is the purpose of copyright legislation?
options: To make all software free
To stop software being sold
To encrypt files
To protect the creator's rights over their work and prevent unauthorised copying
items.answer: To protect the creator's rights over their work and prevent unauthorised copying
items.markingKey: Copyright gives the creator control of copying, distribution and modification.

items.stem: Explain why a company might choose open source software rather than commercial software.
items.answer: No licence fee; the source code can be modified to suit the company's needs; large community support and frequent updates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 2 [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between free software and freeware.
items.answer: Free software gives the freedom to study, modify and share the source code (free as in freedom); freeware is just free of charge, with no access to the source code.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: GreenLeaf Pharmacy buys a licence for 20 users of an accounting package but installs it on 35 computers. Explain the legal issue.
items.answer: Breach of licence agreement and copyright; only 20 installations are allowed; the company could be fined/sued.
items.markingKey: 1 mark breach; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: Lucas downloads a photo-editing program that stops working after 30 days unless a key is bought. Identify the type of licence and give one advantage to the user.
items.answer: Shareware: the user can try it before deciding to pay.
items.markingKey: 1 mark type; 1 mark advantage [2]

items.stem: Ana manages the IT budget at Peak Fitness. Evaluate whether Peak Fitness should use open source software instead of commercial software.
items.answer: Points in favour: no licence cost; source can be adapted and checked for security; community support; no vendor lock-in. Points against / limitations: support may be informal; may need in-house expertise; compatibility with partners' commercial file formats; training costs. Conclusion: depends on in-house skills and need for guaranteed support.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 3 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. Indicative content: no licence cost; source can be adapted and checked for security; community support; no vendor lock-in. / support may be informal; may need in-house expertise; compatibility with partners' commercial file formats; training costs. Shareware
Public domain
Free software

items.stem: Explain why software companies need copyright protection.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: A is false but R is true
items.markingKey: A is false: "Copyright only applies to printed books." is incorrect; R is a true statement.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Free software must always be sold at a low price. Reason (R): Shareware is free to try but must be paid for to continue using it. Which option is correct?

A is false but R is true

items.stem: What is artificial intelligence (AI)?
options: The ability of a computer system to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence
Any program that uses a database
A very fast processor
A robot with a camera
items.answer: The ability of a computer system to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence
items.markingKey: e.g. learning, reasoning, recognising speech or images.

items.stem: Explain one economic advantage and one economic disadvantage of AI for a manufacturing company.
items.answer: Advantage: lower labour costs and faster, more consistent production. Disadvantage: high cost of buying/developing and maintaining AI systems; need for specialist staff.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how bias can arise in AI systems.
items.answer: AI learns from training data; if the data is unrepresentative or reflects past discrimination, the AI repeats it in its decisions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: training data; 1 mark: biased decisions [2]

items.stem: Self-driving delivery vans are being tested in Cape Town. Describe one social and one environmental impact.
items.answer: Social: drivers lose jobs / safety questions; environmental: efficient driving lowers emissions, but more vehicles may be used.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A city council in Toronto uses AI to control traffic lights. Explain one environmental benefit.
items.answer: Smoother traffic flow reduces idling and fuel use, lowering emissions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: GreenLeaf Pharmacy in Lagos is considering investing in AI. Assess the use of AI to make decisions about people, such as loans or medical treatment.
items.answer: Points in favour: consistent, fast decisions; can analyse vast data; may reduce some human errors. Points against / limitations: bias in training data; lack of transparency; accountability for mistakes; privacy. Conclusion: AI should support, not replace, human judgement for decisions about people.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 3 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. Indicative content: consistent, fast decisions; can analyse vast data; may reduce some human errors. / bias in training data; lack of transparency; accountability for mistakes; privacy. [6]

items.stem: Which is an example of AI in everyday use?

A calculator adding numbers
A voice assistant that understands spoken questions
A printer driver

items.markingKey: Speech recognition, recommendation systems, image recognition.

Changes in the types of jobs available
Wider data buses
Faster clock speeds
items.answer: Changes in the types of jobs available
items.markingKey: AI automates routine tasks, creating some jobs and removing others.

Conclusion: the overall effect depends on retraining and government policy.

items.stem: Felix is joining Nova Telecom as a junior software engineer. Discuss, with reasons, the importance of professional codes of conduct for programmers working on safety-critical systems.
items.answer: Points in favour: codes require competence, honesty, public interest; reduce risks to life; maintain public trust; guide difficult decisions. Conclusion: codes are valuable but must be backed by law, testing standards and company culture.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which is an example of AI in everyday use? (b) What is artificial intelligence (AI)?
items.answer: (a) A voice assistant that understands spoken questions (b) The ability of a computer system to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence
items.markingKey: (a) Speech recognition, recommendation systems, image recognition. (b) e.g. learning, reasoning, recognising speech or images.

items.stem: The government in Hanoi is consulting the public about AI. Discuss, with reasons, the impact of artificial intelligence on employment.

Conclusion: the overall effect depends on retraining and government policy.
